conclusion.label: rejects

report:
### Conclusion
Scientific evidence does not support the claim that increasing the number of childhood vaccines causes autism. 

### Key Evidence
* **Cumulative Antigen Exposure:** Studies specifically evaluating whether receiving multiple vaccines ("too many vaccines too soon") increases autism risk show no connection. A study in *The Journal of Pediatrics* evaluated cumulative immunologic stimulation from vaccines during the first two years of life and found no association with autism spectrum disorder (https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2013/03/130329090310.htm).
* **Large Population Analyses:** Extensive epidemiological research, including a study analyzing data from over 650,000 children, found no link between childhood vaccination and autism (https://www.longdom.org/open-access/public-health-perspectives-on-childhood-vaccines-and-autism-110213.html). Similarly, University of Sydney researchers evaluated combination childhood vaccines and found no association with autism (https://www.bioprocessonline.com/doc/study-finds-no-link-between-childhood-vaccines-and-autism-0001).
* **Discredited Origins:** Public concern regarding vaccines and autism largely stems from a small 1998 study of 12 children led by Andrew Wakefield. That study was speculative, poorly designed, and ultimately debunked due to research fraud (https://www.vox.com/2018/2/27/17057990/andrew-wakefield-wakefield-vaccines-autism-study).

While non-consensus studies occasionally claim potential links, overwhelming scientific evidence confirms that neither individual childhood vaccines nor the total vaccine schedule cause autism.
